Abstract
This study aims to enhance the intelligence level of power grid fault analysis to 
address increasingly complex fault scenarios and ensure grid stability and security. 
To this end, an intelligent information system for power grid fault analysis, leveraging 
improved computer communication technology, is proposed and developed. 
The system incorporates a novel fault diagnosis model, combining advanced 
communication technologies such as distributed computing, real-time data 
transmission, cloud computing, and big data analytics, to establish a multi-layered 
information processing architecture for grid fault analysis. Specifically, this study 
introduces a fusion model integrating Transformer self-attention mechanisms with 
graph neural networks (GNNs) based on conventional fault diagnosis techniques. 
GNNs capture the complex relationships between different nodes within the 
grid topology, effectively identifying power transmission characteristics and fault 
propagation paths across grid nodes. The Transformer’s self-attention mechanism 
processes time-series operational data from the grid, enabling precise identification 
of temporal dependencies in fault characteristics. To improve system response speed, 
edge computing moves portions of fault data preprocessing and analysis to edge 
nodes near data sources, significantly reducing transmission latency and enhancing 
real-time diagnosis capability. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed 
model achieves superior diagnostic performance across various fault types (e.g., short 
circuits, overloads, equipment failures) in simulation scenarios. The system achieves 
a fault identification and location accuracy of 99.2%, an improvement of over 10% 
compared to traditional methods, with an average response time of 85 milliseconds, 
approximately 43% faster than existing technologies. Moreover, the system exhibits 
strong robustness in complex scenarios, with an average fault prediction error rate 
of just 1.1% across multiple simulations. This study provides a novel solution for 
intelligent power grid fault diagnosis and management, establishing a technological 
foundation for smart grid operations.

Introduction
With the continuous growth in global energy demand and the increasing complexity of 
power systems, modern power grids face unprecedented challenges. Grid failures hin­
der the steady supply of electricity, often leading to widespread blackouts that result in 
significant economic losses and social impact [1, 2]. Therefore, rapid and accurate fault 
diagnosis and response are critical to ensure the power system’s safe, reliable, and effi­
cient operation. However, traditional grid fault analysis methods have substantial lim­
itations in addressing the contemporary grids’ complexity and dynamic nature. These 
conventional methods typically rely on predefined rules or static models based on his­
torical data, which struggle to handle large volumes of real-time data and fail to effec­
tively capture the grid’s complex topology and spatiotemporal characteristics [3–5]. 
As a result, there is an urgent need to develop new fault diagnosis methods capable of 
meeting the demands of modern power grids. Such methods should integrate advanced 
computing and communication technologies with intelligent algorithms to enhance the 
efficiency and accuracy of grid fault analysis.
In this context, the motivation for this study stems from a thorough understanding 
of complex fault patterns in modern grids and a clear recognition of the limitations of 
current fault-handling technologies. As grid networks expand, intricate interactions and 
dependencies among nodes emerge. A fault in one node can quickly propagate, trigger­
ing chain reactions that may destabilize the entire grid [6, 7]. Thus, effectively capturing 
grid topology and efficiently processing large fault datasets in a short time are core chal­
lenges in grid fault diagnosis. Additionally, recent rapid advances in computer commu­
nication technology have opened up new avenues for power grid fault analysis. Emerging 
algorithms like graph neural networks (GNNs) and Transformer-based self-attention 
mechanisms have demonstrated exceptional potential in processing complex spatiotem­
poral data, making them well-suited for this domain. By integrating these cutting-edge 
algorithms with a distributed architecture combining cloud and edge computing, signifi­
cant improvements in the intelligence of grid fault analysis can be achieved [8–10].
The objective of this study is to develop an intelligent fault diagnosis system for power 
grids by integrating advanced algorithms with distributed computing technology. This 
approach addresses the limitations of traditional methods, which often suffer from inef­
ficiency and diagnostic inaccuracies when dealing with complex grid faults. Specifi­
cally, this study proposes a fusion model based on GNNs and Transformers, designed to 
efficiently capture the topological relationships within the grid and the spatiotemporal 
characteristics of fault propagation. Through a multi-layered architecture that combines 
edge computing with cloud computing, the system can offload part of the computation 
to edge nodes closer to data sources, reducing data transmission latency and enhanc­
ing the system’s real-time response capabilities. Additionally, this intelligent system 
optimizes the processing capabilities of grid fault diagnosis models at the algorithmic 
level, enabling swift responses to various types of faults in dynamic environments. Ulti­
mately, this study improves the accuracy, timeliness, and robustness of grid fault analy­
sis, thereby enhancing the overall efficiency and security of grid operations.

Literature review
In recent years, as power systems expand and electricity demand grows, fault diagno­
sis and analysis technologies for power grids have emerged as a critical area of research 
within power system studies. Numerous scholars have dedicated efforts to enhance the 
efficiency and accuracy of grid fault diagnosis by employing various technologies and 
methodologies. Initially, traditional methods for grid fault diagnosis relied heavily on 
expert systems and rule-based reasoning models. For instance, Li et al. proposed a rule-
based fault diagnosis approach that combined historical grid data with expert knowl­
edge bases to facilitate the rapid identification of common grid faults [11]. However, as 
power grids have expanded in scale, rule-based methods have exhibited notable limita­
tions in handling complex fault scenarios. These methods are particularly prone to infer­
ence deviations when encountering unknown fault types.
To address these limitations, Khaleel et al. introduced artificial intelligence (AI) tech­
niques for grid fault analysis [12]. While AI techniques have somewhat improved diag­
nostic accuracy, the spatiotemporal complexity of grid faults makes it difficult for a 
single AI model to handle the variability in fault types and the dynamic nature of grid 
structures. As machine learning algorithms have evolved, Md Nor et al. developed 
a fault detection method based on Support Vector Machines (SVMs) and data-driven 
approaches [13]. This method leverages the classification capabilities of SVMs to accu­
rately distinguish between fault types, provided sufficient training data is available. How­
ever, its main limitation is the heavy reliance on data volume and the high computational 
costs associated with processing large-scale grid data, restricting its suitability for real-
time fault diagnosis.
Zhou et al. proposed a big data-driven framework for grid fault diagnosis to address 
the challenges of large-scale data processing in power grids. Leveraging distributed 
computing techniques and integrating vast amounts of sensor data within the grid, they 
developed a big data platform capable of real-time monitoring of grid operations [14]. 
While this platform efficiently handles large-scale data, the big data analysis methods 
based on statistical features struggle to capture the complex nonlinear relationships 
within grid systems, limiting their ability to detect anomalous faults effectively. Simi­
larly, Wang et al. underscored the criticality of real-time data analysis and presented a 
method for risk prediction in complex network environments using advanced technolo­
gies. They emphasized data credibility and validity, which directly aligned with the grid 
fault information system’s high accuracy and reliability demands [15]. Recent advance­
ments in GNNs have shown significant progress in handling graph-structured data. Hu 
et al. applied GNNs to grid fault analysis, proposing a GNNs-based diagnostic model 
that leverages the grid’s topological structure for accurate fault localization [16]. Despite 
the clear advantages of the GNN model in processing topological data, it demonstrates 
limitations when dealing with dynamic temporal features in the grid. To address the 
challenge of temporal data processing, Jin et al. incorporated Transformers into grid 
fault analysis, proposing a diagnostic model that combined temporal features with fault 
events. Experimental results indicated that Transformers achieved high accuracy in 
processing temporal power data [17]. However, relying solely on temporal data analysis 
overlooks the grid’s topological structure, limiting the model’s effectiveness in complex 
fault scenarios.

In the context of edge-cloud computing integration, Wang et al. proposed an edge 
computing-based framework for grid fault diagnosis [18]. This approach processed some 
data at edge nodes, reducing the computational load on the central server and enhanc­
ing the real-time handling of faults. Although edge computing increases computational 
efficiency, a standalone edge computing model may still face limitations when manag­
ing complex fault analysis tasks, highlighting the need for collaborative integration with 
cloud computing. The literature survey is exhibited in Table 1.
In light of the limitations in previous research, this study proposes an innovative solu­
tion that utilizes GNNs to capture complex relationships in the grid’s topology while 
leveraging Transformers to process the grid’s temporal data, enabling precise fault diag­
nosis. Additionally, it introduces a collaborative edge-cloud computing architecture, 
where edge nodes perform partial data processing to alleviate the computational bur­
den on central servers, significantly enhancing system real-time performance and fault 
response capabilities.

Methodology
Overall architecture design of the smart grid fault diagnosis information system
The overall architecture of the smart grid fault diagnosis information system is illustrated 
in Fig. 1. The system is structured into four primary layers: data acquisition, communica­
tion and transmission, edge computing, and central control layers. Through distributed 
computing and communication technologies, these layers work in close coordination to 
enable real-time monitoring and diagnosis of faults.
The data acquisition layer encompasses sensors, smart meters, and intelligent moni­
toring devices installed at various nodes throughout the grid. These devices enable 
real-time monitoring of operational parameters, such as voltage, current, power, and 
frequency, and transmit the collected data to the communication layer using Internet 
of Things (IoT) technology. At this layer, the accuracy and immediacy of data collec­
tion are foundational for precise fault diagnosis within the system. Sensors in this layer 
are categorized into two types: local and global sensors. Local sensors, deployed primar­
ily at key nodes like transformers and switch stations, gather operational data specific 
to those nodes; global sensors are distributed along the grid’s main transmission lines, 
monitoring the overall status of power transmission. At the core of the data acquisi­
tion layer is a data accuracy model, which ensures that the collected data aligns with 
the input requirements of the diagnostic model. The communication layer is tasked with 
fast and reliable data transmission from the data acquisition layer to the edge comput­
ing layer and central control center. This layer utilizes high-speed fiber-optic networks

Dtotal = Dtrans + Dprop + Dproc + Dqueue 
(1)
Dtrans, Dprop, and Dqueue represent data transmission latency, signal propagation

By optimizing transmission paths and protocols within the communication network, 
these latencies can be minimized, thereby enhancing the system’s response speed. The 
edge computing layer is designed to reduce data transmission loads and alleviate the 
computational burden on the central control layer. This layer uses edge computing tech­
nology for preliminary data processing and analysis by positioning high-capacity servers 
near data sources at edge nodes. Specifically, simple rules or machine learning models 
are employed to filter anomalous data points, and fault detection algorithms based on 
local grid topology provide an initial assessment of faults at nodes or along transmis­
sion lines. Only essential data are transmitted from the edge nodes to the central control 
center, which reduces bandwidth requirements. A key advantage of the edge computing 
layer is its significant improvement in real-time responsiveness. The computation model 
utilized at edge nodes in this system can be written as Eq. (2).
Tedge = Tdata + Tcalc + Ttrans 
(2)
Tdata stands for the data reception time at the edge node, Tcalc refers to the compu­
tation time, and Ttrans represents the transmission time from the edge to the central 
control center. By optimizing both computation and transmission processes, the overall 
system response time is markedly reduced.
The central control layer, deployed in the cloud, serves as the system’s core compu­
tation and control unit. Its primary function is to conduct in-depth fault analysis and 
global optimization based on data transmitted from the data acquisition and edge com­
puting layers. The main components of the central control layer include: (1) Fault Diag­
nosis Engine: This engine employs a GNN-Transformer fusion model to perform global 
fault diagnosis and localization based on network-wide data. The GNN captures the 
topological features of the grid, while the Transformer processes the sequential data of 
grid operations. (2) Fault Reporting and Optimization Module: Following fault analysis, 
the system generates a fault report and provides optimal handling strategies to guide 
maintenance personnel in rapid response. The core calculation of the global fault diag­
nosis model is shown in Eq. (3):
Fdiag = GNN (Datatopo) + Transformer (Dataseq) 
(3)
GNN (Datatopo) represents processing the grid topology data based on GNNs; 
Transformer (Dataseq) denotes the processing of sequential operational data using 
the self-attention mechanism of the Transformer. This fused model enables efficient and 
accurate fault localization and diagnosis, even in complex fault scenarios.

The system uses distributed computing technology to allocate numerous compu­
tational tasks across various multiple nodes, mainly for processing data from the data 
acquisition and edge computing layers. Distributed data processing supports the parallel 
handling of large-scale grid data, enhancing overall performance. High-speed transmis­

time data transmission, ensuring that fault data within the grid is quickly sent to the

under high-fault frequency conditions, the edge computing layer alleviates the load on 
the central computing layer. The cloud computing-based central control layer processes 
large-scale grid data, conducts fault analysis, and performs optimization. Additionally, 
big data analytics help the system extract useful patterns and features from historical 
grid operation data, further enhancing diagnostic accuracy.

damental unit of GNNs is the message-passing mechanism, whereby each node updates 
its features through information exchange with neighboring nodes [22, 23]. For each

In power grid fault diagnosis, GNNs can effectively capture the network’s topological 
properties, especially amid complex interactions between multiple nodes. For example, 
during faults like short circuits or overloads, the association strength between nodes 
may vary significantly. Using the message-passing mechanism, the GNN model can 
sense these changes, providing crucial feature support for fault analysis. Additionally, 
power transmission within the grid exhibits pronounced directionality and weighted 
characteristics. Therefore, it is essential to incorporate edge weights in GNNs, enabling 
node connections to reflect neighboring nodes and physical attributes, such as resis­
tance or voltage drops. The message passing in the weighted GNNs model is described 
in Eq. (6):

Since data in power grids exhibits strong temporal characteristics, it is essential to 
account for fault features along the time dimension. The Transformer model has demon­
strated superior performance in handling sequential data, especially in capturing long-
range dependencies. The Transformer consists primarily of self-attention mechanisms 
and feed-forward neural networks. Unlike traditional recurrent neural networks (RNNs), 
the Transformer uses self-attention to process each timestep in parallel, significantly 
enhancing computational efficiency. The core idea behind self-attention is to compute 
the relevance between different positions within a sequence, weighting each timestep’s 
input features accordingly [24, 25]. For an input sequence X = (x1, x2, · · · , xn), self-
attention is calculated as Eq. (7):

Q, K, and V represent the query, key, and value matrices, derived through linear trans­
formations. They indicate the mapping of the input sequence into different spaces. 
Here, dk denotes the dimension of the key matrix, typically used for normalization. The 
softmax function calculates the attention weights, transforming the level of attention 
each timestep pays to others into a probability distribution. Through the self-attention 
mechanism, the Transformer can effectively capture long-range dependencies in the 
operational data of power grids, such as the temporal patterns of current fluctuations 
before and after a fault occurs.
In grid fault diagnosis, temporal data—such as the variations in current and voltage 
over time—serves as critical fault characteristics. The Transformer model leverages self-
attention to extract potential temporal dependency features from this sequential data. 
For instance, fluctuations in the current at a specific node can signal an impending fault 
at that node. By incorporating positional encoding, the Transformer retains sequen­
tial information, ensuring that temporal features are effectively represented within the 
model. The strength of the Transformer in processing sequential data lies in its ability to 
capture long-range dependencies between timesteps and its superior parallel computa­
tion capabilities compared to traditional RNNs and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) 
models. Consequently, when analyzing temporal features in power grid data, the Trans­
former can more accurately identify fault signals within the grid.
To integrate the topological features of the power grid with temporal characteristics, 
an experimental design involving a GNN-Transformer fusion model has been developed. 
This model can simultaneously capture the complex interrelations within the grid’s topo­
logical structure and the temporal dependency features present in the sequential data. 
In Fig. 2, the fusion model consists of two main pathways: the GNN pathway processes

the topological structure of the grid, taking as input the connection information and 
weights between grid nodes, and outputs the fault-related feature vectors for each node. 
Moreover, the Transformer pathway handles the sequential operational data of the grid,

these features are combined with the temporal data and fed into the Transformer for 
further analysis. The final output of the Transformer is utilized to generate fault predic­
tion results, encompassing predictions of fault locations and timings.
This study employs a joint training strategy to optimize the collaborative functioning 
of GNNs and Transformers. The node feature extraction process of GNNs and the tem­
poral feature extraction process of the Transformer share certain parameters, which are 
optimized through a combined loss function during training. The overall loss function is 
defined as Eq. (8):
Ltotal =∝LGNN + β LT ransformer 
(8)
LGNN is the loss function for GNNs, designed to minimize the classification error for 
node faults; LT ransformer represents the loss function for the Transformer, which mea­
sures the prediction error of temporal faults. The coefficients ∝ and β  serve as weight­
ing factors to balance the contributions of the two-loss components.
During the inference phase of fault analysis, the system first utilizes GNNs to analyze 
the topological structure of the power grid, identifying potential fault nodes and propa­
gation paths. Subsequently, the Transformer analyzes the temporal data to determine 
the timing characteristics of the faults, further pinpointing the specific location and

In the context of power grid fault diagnosis, GNNs and Transformer models excel at 
handling different types of data. GNNs are primarily adept at processing power grid 
topology data, while Transformers demonstrate superior performance in dealing with 
time series data. To leverage both strengths, a GNN-Transformer fusion model is 
designed to capture the topological and temporal characteristics of the power grid, thus 
enhancing the accuracy and robustness of fault diagnosis. GNNs can effectively capture 
the relationships between various nodes in the power grid through a message-passing 
mechanism. In power grid fault diagnosis, the power grid topology, which includes 
transformers, switch stations, transmission lines, etc., forms the basic structure of the 
network. GNNs can learn the connections between these nodes, capturing fault propa­
gation paths and power transmission characteristics between nodes. Through multiple 
layers of message passing, GNNs can progressively update the feature representation 
of each node, ultimately extracting graph structural features that aid in fault diagnosis. 
Concurrently, changes in power grid operational data, such as current and voltage, often 
exhibit significant temporal characteristics. These temporal data reflect the dynamic 
behavior of the power grid before and after a fault occurs. The Transformer model can 
effectively capture long-range dependencies in such temporal data through its self-
attention mechanism. Unlike traditional RNNs, Transformers can process data at each 
time step in parallel, improve computational efficiency, and handle complex temporal 
dependencies in long sequences, thereby precisely identifying feature patterns before 
and after a fault. In the proposed fusion model, GNNs and Transformers process the 
topological and temporal features of the power grid, respectively, and fuse these two 
types of features. Specifically, the GNN first processes the power grid topology data to 
generate feature representations for each node. Subsequently, these node features, along 
with temporal data such as changes in current and voltage, are fed into the Transformer 
model as inputs. The Transformer further extracts dynamic change features from the 
temporal data through its self-attention mechanism, eventually combining with the 
topological features extracted by the GNN to form a unified feature representation. Dur­
ing the fusion process, the GNN and Transformer models share certain parameters, 
which are optimized through joint training to work more effectively in tandem. Through 
such fusion, GNNs provide a global perspective of the topological structure, identify­
ing paths of fault propagation; Transformers capture the temporal characteristics of fault 
occurrence by processing temporal data, enabling the model to offer more precise diag­
nostic results when faced with complex fault patterns. This fusion model demonstrates 
significant advantages in power grid fault diagnosis. Firstly, it considers both the static 
topological structure and dynamic temporal features of the power grid simultaneously, 
achieving a more comprehensive fault diagnosis. Traditional fault diagnosis methods 
often focus on either topological or temporal information, leading to suboptimal per­
formance in complex fault scenarios. The proposed model greatly enhances diagnostic 
accuracy by combining the strengths of both. In various simulated scenarios, the pro­
posed model has shown stronger diagnostic capabilities than using GNN or Transformer 
alone, particularly in complex multi-fault scenarios, where diagnostic accuracy has been 
significantly improved. Secondly, power grid faults can quickly affect large areas, making 
the rapid and accurate identification of fault locations and types crucial for ensuring grid

Collaborative architecture design of edge computing and cloud computing
Edge computing refers to deploying data processing and analytical capabilities closer to 
the data source, such as edge devices (e.g., smart sensors, routers, gateways, etc.). By 
performing preliminary data processing at the edge, the demand for data transmission to 
the cloud is significantly reduced, thus lowering latency and enhancing the system’s real-
time performance. In Fig. 3, the architecture of edge computing can effectively facilitate 
the data flow from the device layer to the edge layer and then to the cloud layer, estab­
lishing a multi-tiered processing system.
Cloud computing provides robust computational and storage capabilities, making it 
suitable for large-scale data analysis and model training. In the context of power grid 
fault analysis, cloud computing can perform deep learning on historical data to enhance 
the accuracy of fault prediction models. However, relying solely on cloud computing 
may lead to latencies and bandwidth bottlenecks.
Based on power grid fault analysis, this study designs a collaborative model integrating 
edge-cloud computing to achieve more efficient fault detection and processing. The col­
laborative process between edge computing and cloud computing is outlined in Table 3.
Experimental environment
A comprehensive experimental platform is constructed to validate the feasibility and 
performance of the proposed intelligent information system in practical applications. 
This platform primarily consists of several hardware components. Firstly, the central 
control server is equipped with an Intel Xeon E5-2670 @2.60 GHz processor, 128 Giga­
Byte (GB) Double Data Rate (DDR4) memory, and 2 TeraByte (TB) SSD NVMe storage. 
Moreover, an NVIDIA Tesla V100 Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) is employed to accel­
erate the training and inference of deep learning models. The edge computing nodes are 
configured with an Intel Core i7-9700 K @3.60 GHz processor, 32 GB DDR4 memory, 
and 512 GB SSD storage. Meanwhile, it utilizes Raspberry Pi 4 Model B as edge devices

enhancing accuracy, the proposed model also notably reduces computation time.
The system response times under different computational architectures are sug­
gested in Fig. 5. Utilizing edge computing significantly reduces response times, decreas­
ing the response time from 150 ms in cloud computing to 65 ms. The data indicates 
that processing close to the data source has a marked impact on enhancing real-time 
performance.
The energy consumption comparisons across various computational architectures are 
revealed in Fig. 6. Edge computing and hybrid computing architectures demonstrate a 
remarkable advantage in energy consumption over cloud computing while maintaining 
system efficiency.

Conclusion
This study successfully establishes an intelligent power grid fault analysis informa­
tion system based on improved computer communication technologies. By integrating 
GNNs and Transformer models, the system remarkably enhances the accuracy and real-
time performance of power grid fault diagnosis. Experimental results indicate that the 
proposed GNNs-Transformer model achieves an accuracy of 99.2% in power grid fault 
diagnosis. It represents a notable improvement over the standalone GNNs model while 
effectively reducing computation time. Furthermore, after introducing edge computing 
technology, the system’s response time decreases from 150 ms in cloud computing to 65 
ms, and energy consumption is optimized. Despite these achievements, the study has

Abstract: This study aims to enhance the intelligence level of power grid fault analysis to address increasingly complex fault scenarios and ensure grid stability and security. To this end, an intelligent information system for power grid fault analysis, leveraging improved computer communication technology, is proposed and developed. The system incorporates a novel fault diagnosis model, combining advanced communication technologies such as distributed computing, real-time data transmission, cloud computing, and big data analytics, to establish a multi-layered information processing architecture for grid fault analysis. Specifically, this study introduces a fusion model integrating Transformer self-attention mechanisms with graph neural networks (GNNs) based on conventional fault diagnosis techniques. GNNs capture the complex relationships between different nodes within the grid topology, effectively identifying power transmission characteristics and fault propagation paths across grid nodes. The Transformer’s self-attention mechanism processes time-series operational data from the grid, enabling precise identification of temporal dependencies in fault characteristics. To improve system response speed, edge computing moves portions of fault data preprocessing and analysis to edge nodes near data sources, significantly reducing transmission latency and enhancing real-time diagnosis capability. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves superior diagnostic performance across various fault types (e.g., short circuits, overloads, equipment failures) in simulation scenarios. The system achieves a fault identification and location accuracy of 99.2%, an improvement of over 10% compared to traditional methods, with an average response time of 85 milliseconds, approximately 43% faster than existing technologies. Moreover, the system exhibits strong robustness in complex scenarios, with an average fault prediction error rate of just 1.1% across multiple simulations. This study provides a novel solution for intelligent power grid fault diagnosis and management, establishing a technological foundation for smart grid operations.
